approachQuestion.prompt:
Smallest joined identifier

Given nonempty strings made only of decimal digits, order them so their concatenation is lexicographically smallest. Return the concatenated string. Leading zeroes are allowed; keep every input string exactly once.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 100,000; each string has between 1 and 1,000 characters. The caller’s input array and strings must remain unchanged.

Examples: ["3","30","34","5","9"] → "3033459". ["12","121"] → "12112".

Choose a valid method that meets the full contract with the least unnecessary work.
constraints: The stated input/output and mutation requirements apply to every option.

options.text: Sort strings with comparator a before b exactly when a+b is lexicographically smaller than b+a, then concatenate.
options.feedback: The pairwise concatenation comparison decides which adjacent order yields the smaller combined result.

options.text: Sort by numeric value ascending, then concatenate.
options.feedback: Numeric order does not minimize joined text: ["3","30"] should become "303", not "330".

options.text: Sort by string length ascending, then concatenate.
Try every permutation and keep the smallest concatenation.
options.feedback: This is correct but enumerates factorially many orders; sorting with the pairwise rule avoids permutation enumeration.

feedback.reason: For two IDs a,b, compare a+b with b+a to decide which local order makes the whole join smaller.
details: Copy the string references and use comparison merge sort with the a+b versus b+a comparator, building both temporary concatenations for each comparison. Then append the strings in order into a preallocated result buffer.

For two IDs a,b, compare a+b with b+a to decide which local order makes the whole join smaller. Character construction is not a constant-time key comparison; those temporary concatenations belong in the cost model.

“Sort strings with comparator a before b exactly when a+b is lexicographically smaller than b+a, then concatenate.”: The pairwise concatenation comparison decides which adjacent order yields the smaller combined result.
“Sort by numeric value ascending, then concatenate.”: Numeric order does not minimize joined text: ["3","30"] should become "303", not "330".
“Sort by string length ascending, then concatenate.”: Length alone fails: ["12","121"] should be "12112".
“Try every permutation and keep the smallest concatenation.”: This is correct but enumerates factorially many orders; sorting with the pairwise rule avoids permutation enumeration.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze the revealed comparison merge-sort method. Let n be the number of strings and m the maximum string length. Each comparison constructs both concatenations a+b and b+a, copying their characters, then compares them. Count the final concatenation buffer as additional memory along with copied string references, the linear merge buffer, temporary concatenations, and logarithmic recursion stack; exclude only caller input. Copying or comparing one character costs constant time. Use a preallocated result buffer and choose tight worst-case bounds in n and m over all allowed inputs.

options.text: O(m n log n) time, O(m n + n) additional space
O(n log n) time, O(n) additional space
O(m n²) time, O(m n + n) additional space
O(m n) time, O(m) additional space

feedback.reason: Include string construction per comparison and the separate result buffer.
details: Merge sort makes a worst-case comparison count proportional to n log n. Building both concatenations costs up to m characters per comparison (constant factors suppressed); inputs with n strings of length m realize this bound. The result may contain m n characters; reference arrays use linear space, temporary comparisons use O(m), and the recursion stack O(log n). Constant-time comparison omits character copying; quadratic comparison count is not tight; linear time omits sorting and O(m) memory omits the result buffer.
